questions.enonce_markdown:
6. How and Why did a civil war break out in the 1960s **either** (a) The Congo **or** (b) Nigeria?
What was the outcome of the civil war in the country chosen?

**(6/7/7 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
(The candidate answers for ONE country only. Both are given below as model answers.)

---

## (a) The Congo (1960-1965)

**How the crisis broke out (6 marks).**
- The Belgian Congo became independent on **30 June 1960**, with **Joseph Kasavubu** as President and **Patrice Lumumba** as Prime Minister.
- Within days (5 July) the **Force Publique**, still commanded by Belgian officers, mutinied against its Belgian officers; there was violence against Europeans, many of whom fled, and Belgium sent troops to protect them (10 July).
- On **11 July 1960** **Moïse Tshombe** declared the rich copper province of **Katanga** independent, and **South Kasai** (Albert Kalonji) soon followed.
- Lumumba asked the United Nations for help, and then turned to the Soviet Union; the UN sent a peacekeeping force (ONUC). In September 1960 President Kasavubu dismissed Lumumba, who dismissed him in return; Colonel **Joseph-Désiré Mobutu** seized power briefly. Lumumba was arrested and was killed in Katanga in January 1961.

**Why it broke out (7 marks).**
- **Lack of preparation.** Belgium had trained very few Congolese administrators, officers or graduates, and independence was granted quickly; the state had almost no experienced Congolese officials.
- **Ethnic and regional divisions.** The Congo is huge and its peoples were divided (the Bakongo, Baluba, Lunda and others); Katanga and Kasai wanted to keep their own wealth.
- **Economic interests.** Foreign mining companies (such as the Union Minière in Katanga) and Belgium supported secession to protect their interests.
- **Political rivalries.** Quarrels between Lumumba and Kasavubu and between parties divided the government.
- **The Army mutiny.** The Force Publique remained under Belgian officers after independence; the soldiers wanted Africanisation of the officer corps.
- **Cold War rivalry.** Lumumba's appeal to the USSR made the West suspicious, and the great powers took sides.

**Outcome (7 marks).**
- The UN forces helped to end the secession of Katanga in **January 1963**, and the United Nations left in 1964.
- New revolts (the Simba rebellion of 1964, in the east) broke out and were put down with Belgian and American help.
- On **24 November 1965** General Mobutu seized power; he ruled a united Congo as a one-party dictatorship for more than thirty years.
- Thousands of people died, the economy was damaged, Lumumba became a symbol of African nationalism, and the Congo crisis showed the weakness of the UN and the danger of Cold War interference in Africa.

---

## (b) Nigeria (1967-1970)

**How the war broke out (6 marks).**
- In **January 1966** a group of young army officers, mostly Igbo, overthrew the government and killed several northern and western leaders, including the Prime Minister Tafawa Balewa. General **Aguiyi-Ironsi**, an Igbo, took power.
- In **July 1966** northern officers staged a counter-coup, Ironsi was killed and Lieutenant-Colonel **Yakubu Gowon** became head of state. In the following months thousands of Igbo living in the North were killed and many fled to the East.
- Colonel **Odumegwu Ojukwu**, the military governor of the Eastern Region, refused to recognise Gowon. A meeting at **Aburi** (Ghana, January 1967) failed to settle the crisis.
- On 27 May 1967 Gowon divided the country into twelve states, breaking up the Eastern Region; on **30 May 1967** Ojukwu declared the independence of the **Republic of Biafra**. Federal forces attacked in July 1967 and the war began.

**Why it broke out (7 marks).**
- **Ethnic and regional rivalry** between the three main groups, the Hausa-Fulani in the North, the Yoruba in the West and the Igbo in the East, built into the three-region federation inherited from the colonial period.
- **Political quarrels and coups.** The disputed elections and the unrest of 1964-1965, followed by the coups of 1966, destroyed trust.
- **Killings of the Igbo** in the North in 1966, which convinced the Igbo that they were not safe in Nigeria.
- **Oil.** The oil of the Niger Delta lay in the East, which made the revenue-sharing dispute more serious.
- **Failure of the negotiations** at Aburi and the creation of states, which Ojukwu saw as a plot to deprive the East of its oil.

**Outcome (7 marks).**
- The federal army, with the help of Britain and the Soviet Union, blockaded Biafra; Biafra lacked food and the people suffered **famine**; some countries and relief organisations helped Biafra. Many people died, from fighting, hunger and disease; estimates vary from several hundred thousand to over a million.
- Biafra surrendered in **January 1970** (15 January) and Ojukwu fled abroad.
- Gowon proclaimed "**no victor, no vanquished**" and launched the policy of the three Rs: **Reconciliation, Rehabilitation and Reconstruction**.
- Nigeria remained one country and the army kept power for years; the war left bitterness among the Igbo, and made Nigerians aware of the danger of ethnic division.
